Ecobiological approach to research regarding ageing and diseases

Ageing and age-related diseases (ARD) share a common biological clock that appears as their root cause: protein damage. A majority of proteins have evolved into native structures resistant to oxidative damage but any folding imperfections, including those due to “silent” amino acid substitutions, reduce oxidation resistance. Damaged proteins accumulate with age and trigger ageing-like phenotypes reversible by their turnover, while acquired genome alterations remain as stable consequences of protein malfunction. Ageing and ARD display species-specific latency in phenotypic expression. Disease latency may be proposed as to be due to phenotypic suppression of cellular defects by molecular traffic among neighbouring cells. Such cross-complementation of functional deficiencies acts as a kind of tissue-based cellular “solidarity”, called cellular parabiosis. Chronic inflammation reveals dormant cell phenotypes and shortens disease latency by the breakdown of cell-cell communication, as in tumour promotion and inflammation. At the present time, predictive diagnostics, prognostics, prevention and even cure of disease by phenotypic reversion become conceivable.
Key words: ecobiology, carbonylation, DNA, protein damage, reactive oxygen species, cellular parabiosis
Introduction
Ecobiology can be defined as an approach that investigates the interconnections and communication between cells and between cells and their internal (within the body) and external environments.

For decades, research has been focused on diseases related to ageing as opposed to the ageing process itself. Still too much research is concerned with studying and treating the consequences rather than the causes of ageing and agerelated diseases (ARD). There are many mechanisms for protecting, repairing and maintaining the cells, but ageing still occurs with species-specific speed. The key to unlocking treatments to extend healthy life may come from research on mechanisms that provide protection against incurring damage, in particular protein damage, because proteins carry on all life processes - directly or by synthesizing, modifying and repairing other molecules, including proteins. Maintaining protein activity means maintaining life, and living species differ greatly in their success regarding maintaining functional proteomes.

Thus, death may not be indispensable and diseases may not be unavoidable. Several death and disease-resistant species have been described in the literature. Deinococcus radiodurans and Bdelloid rotifers resist desiccation and massive radiation, the marine medusa Turritopsis nutricula reproduces without ageing, a tardigrade is resistant to desiccation and radiation, and survives both in space (in a vacuum at $- 2 7 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ and when exposed to very high UV-C and cosmic rays, and, finally, the naked mole rat is able to live for more than 30 years without cancer. Even the ability to repair excessively damaged DNA was described as being dependent on the protection of standard repair proteins against oxidative damage [1-5].

To explain the concept that protein damage, in particular the irreversible protein carbonylation (PC), determines ageing and ARD was promoted in 2016 [6]. According to the author, the first bottleneck in cell recovery from radiation damage is functional (proteome) rather than informational (DNA), since prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell death correlates with incurred protein, but not DNA, damage by reactive oxygen species (ROS). Proteome protection against oxidative damage determines survival after ionizing or UV irradiation, since sufficient residual proteome activity is required to turn on the DNA damage response activating DNA repair and protein renewal processes. The observation that oxidative damage targeted selectively to cellular proteins results in ageing-like phenotypes suggests that ageing and age-related diseases could be phenotypic consequences of proteome damage patterns progressing with age.

The limits to protein protection result in mistakes in DNA maintenance and replication (mutations) as well as in the maintenance of epigenetic DNA modification (methylation) that cause “silent” but stable change called initiation of disease. Initiated disease can remain latent for decades until disease promotion – usually chronic inflammation – leads to the expressed onset of disease.

The aim of the present article is to present the interconnections and communication between cells, and between cells and their external environment, with regards to PC and its impact on the process of ageing and ARD.
Methods

The author conducted an exhaustive literature review regarding ecobiology, DNA repair, reactive oxygen species, protein carbonylation and cell homeostasis via cellular parabiosis. Results were presented at the World Rendezvous on Dermatology, on November 2nd, 2018 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
Results

PC is irreversible oxidative damage, often leading to a loss of protein function, considered to be a widespread indicator of severe oxidative damage and disease-causing protein dysfunction [7]. Already in 1987, PC was shown to be closely associated with ageing and with the longevity of diverse species [8].

Since carbonylated proteins (CP) correlate with and become a suspected cause of morbidity and mortality, there is a need for their accurate quantification and localization. To this end, carbonyls in proteins, lipids and DNA from cell extracts have been used as biomarkers of oxidative stress and ageing [9]. While moderate amounts of CP are degraded by the proteasomal system, high amounts of CP tend to form high-molecular-weight aggregates that are resistant to degradation and accumulate as damaged unfolded proteins inhibiting the proteasome activity and becoming potentially cytotoxic [7].

A large number of neurodegenerative diseases are directly associated with the accumulation of proteolysis-resistant aggregates of CP in tissues [10-13]. Identification of specific functionally impaired CP and development of selective carbonyl blockers should lead to a causative assessment, possibly providing new therapeutic approaches [7].

The fact that genes can affect the rate of ageing supports the idea that there are multiple causes of ageing [14]. Research has focused on interventions that extend the maximal longevity of an organism, meaning that the affected pathway is a bottleneck in the ageing process. The finding that the TOR inhibitor rapamycin extended longevity, even when administered late in the lifespan of a mouse, is the first clear example of targeting ageing and addressing age-related diseases [15]. Today, rapamycin is a FDAapproved mTOR inhibitor exhibiting significant anti-cancer and anti-ageing properties. While PC is well characterized, the overall biology of oxidative protein modifications is complex and still needs to be understood [16].
Reactive oxygen species

The existence of free radicals, as chemical entities, was shown over 100 years ago, but their biological impact is far from clear. The existence and importance of free radicals in biological systems was not recognized until the mid1950s by a small number of visionary scientists who can be credited with founding the field of reactive oxygen biochemistry. For most of the remaining 20th century, ROS were considered as a type of biochemical “rusting agent” that caused stochastic tissue damage and disease. Currently, it is recognized that virtually every disease state involves some degree of oxidative stress. Moreover, ROS appear to be generated in a well-regulated manner to help maintain homeostasis on the cellular level in normal, healthy tissue [17].

text: ROS are constantly generated within cells at low concentrations under physiological conditions, playing a part in cellular redox regulation. Cellular production of ROS occurs from both enzymatic and non-enzymatic processes [18, 19]. But, they can also be the outcome of acute cell stresses and may result in cell death via apoptosis or necrosis. Proteins are major biological targets for ROS and secondary by-products of oxidative stress when these are formed in vivo either in intra- or extracellular environments, as they are the major component of most biological systems and can scavenge 50 to $7 5 \%$ of reactive radicals such as -OH [20]. Some ROS-induced protein modifications occur preferentially to misfolded proteins and then provoke further unfolding of the protein structure, while some are essentially harmless events [21]. Irreversible protein modifications usually lead to inactivation of protein activities and interactions with other proteins or molecules and may result in harmful cellular effects and diseases [7]. More recently, Krisko and Radman showed that evolved structural resistance of proteins may protect from oxidation, thus showing a competitive antagonism between folding and oxidation [1].

Tissue homeostasis by “cellular parabiosis”

Originally, parabiosis was used to investigate the influences of an organism on its conjoined partner and scientists came up with an animal model that essentially copies the natural phenomenon of conjoined twins [22]. Nowadays, this model may also be adapted to cell and tissue homeostasis. “Cellular parabiosis” may be considered a means of cell solidarity and intercellular communication, playing a major role in tissue homeostasis and responses to external cues [23].

The process of cellular parabiosis seems to have been a highly conserved evolutionary process. Higher eukaryotes use several means of intercellular communication to address both the changing physiological demands of the body and to fight against diseases. In recent years, there has been increasing interest in understanding how cell-derived nano-vesicles, known as extracellular vesicles (EVs), can function as normal paracrine mediators of intercellular communication, but can also elicit disease progression and may be used for innovative therapies.

Recently, novel structures for intercellular communication have been described [24]. These tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) consist of thin-extended membrane protrusions that connect cells together. TNTs allow the cell-to-cell transfer of various cellular components, including proteins, RNAs, viruses, and organelles, such as mitochondria [23]. TNTs are a different means of communication to classical gap junctions or cell fusions and represent the process of heteroplasmy. The role of EVs in cell communication is relatively well-understood, but how TNTs fit into this process is just emerging [25].

As an example, cellular parabiosis may first lead to long cancer latency by suppressing the malignant phenotype of a single cell (by parabiosis with non-malignant neighbouring cells) while chronic inflammation destroys cell-cell communication and leads to cancer growth. Cellular parabiosis within the tumour seems to bestow tumour fitness. The principle of cellular parabiosis in suppressing the diseased cellular phenotype is shown in figure 2.

There is an old argument in favour of the recent cellular parabiosis hypothesis. Already in 1981, Newbold and Amos showed that the inflammatory molecule 12-Otetradecanoyl-phorbol-13-acetate (TPA), the most potent known tumour promoter, almost totally reversed the effect of wild-type cells on mutant recovery when included in the medium at concentrations as low as $1 \mathrm { n M }$ . TPA also markedly enhanced the expression, in crowded cultures, of HPRT- mutants induced by the carcinogen N-methylN-nitrosourea. This property was not shared by other phorbol esters which are inactive as tumour promoters, or by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons [26]. Thus, phenotypic suppression of new and of expressed old recessive mutations is prevented by TPA.
Discussion and conclusion

Cellular life is maintained by protein activities preventing molecular damage and repairing damaged DNA, proteins and other damaged cellular components. Cellular fitness decreases due to the fact that these proteins are themselves subject to damage, leading to the progressive degeneracy of cellular functions due to diminishing protein activity and decreased precision of macromolecular biosynthesis. The ultimate liability to protein function is the irreversible oxidative protein modification, also called PC [1, 8, 27]. Since cellular ageing can be defined as a progressive degeneration and even loss of almost all vital cellular functions, and an increase in mutation rates, oxidative proteome damage may be the most likely cause of ageing and ARD, including cancer [1]. text: Thus, with PC being the best available biomarker of ageing, together with other protein damage features, it appears as its most likely cause [1, 8]. Therefore, it is plausible that functional and mutagenic consequences of PC also apply to human cells. As a result, oxidative proteome damage becomes a lead candidate for a common, preventable, underlying cause of ageing and age-related diseases.

In conclusion, understanding the root causes of the initially latent cell dysfunction as being the result of the failures of damaged proteins and all means of intercellular molecular traffic compensating for cell defects, as the determinant of the onset of latent diseases, may become a landmark for the future prevention and healing (by disease reversion) of ARD and its associated conditions. -
